metadata.title: R3: Media Amplification
metadata.description: Modern media business models reward content that wins attention. Emotional content wins more attention than careful analysis. As trust falls, audiences demand more outrage — and producers supply it.
metadata.author: US Government Intelligent Textbook

nodes.label: Emotionally Charged Media
nodes.description: News and social-media content selected to provoke strong reactions — outrage, fear, validation.

nodes.label: Audience Attention Competition
nodes.description: Market pressure among outlets to win finite human attention.

nodes.label: Sensationalism
nodes.description: The choice to amplify dramatic framings over careful analysis — a competitive outcome of the attention market.

nodes.label: Public Frustration
nodes.description: Citizens' sense of being unheard, exhausted, or alarmed — the same node that connects R2 and R3 in the full system.

nodes.label: Trust In Government
nodes.description: The percentage of citizens who say they trust the federal government to do what is right.

nodes.label: Demand for Outrage Media
nodes.description: Audience appetite for content that confirms the worst about the other side. Rises when trust falls.

edges.description: Emotional content wins attention; competitors must match it or lose audience.
Sustained attention competition rewards the most provocative framings.
A sensational news environment leaves citizens anxious and unable to distinguish signal from noise.
Frustration and anxiety pull trust down.
When trust in mainstream institutions falls, audiences seek content that confirms their worst suspicions.
Audience demand for outrage content shapes what producers make more of.

loops.label: R3: Media Amplification
loops.description: The attention market reinforces distrust because outrage drives engagement.
